entities.name: Kamal al-Din ibn al-Humam
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Kamal al-Din Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahid al-Siwasi al-Hanafi, known as Ibn al-Humam (died 1457 CE in Cairo), was an unparalleled Egyptian Hanafi-Maturidi polymath whose comprehensive mastery across diverse Islamic sciences established him as a paramount legal theorist and jurist of the late Mamluk Sultanate. Revered as a mujtahid, or independent interpreter of Islamic law, his intellectual contributions bridged the fields of fiqh (jurisprudence), usul al-fiqh (legal theory), kalam (speculative theology), and Sufism, profoundly influencing subsequent generations of scholars in the Sunni Islamic world. His era, characterized by intellectual consolidation within the Mamluk domain, found in Ibn al-Humam a figure who synthesized vast knowledge traditions, thereby solidifying the intellectual foundations of the Hanafi school.

Ibn al-Humam's monumental work, *Fath al-Qadir*, a multi-volume commentary on al-Marghinani's *al-Hidaya*, became an indispensable reference for Hanafi jurists, systematically elucidating complex legal principles and offering incisive critiques. Beyond jurisprudence, his intellectual prowess extended to logic, Arabic language and literature, tafsir (Qur'anic exegesis), Hadith studies, and even mathematics and music, demonstrating a holistic approach to knowledge acquisition characteristic of medieval Islamic scholarship. He also authored significant treatises on kalam, such as *al-Musayara fi al-Aqa'id al-Munjiyah fi al-Akhirah*, which articulated Maturidi theological positions with exceptional clarity and rigor.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Kamal al-Din ibn al-Humam profoundly shaped Hanafi jurisprudence and Maturidi theology through his comprehensive commentaries and original treatises, establishing standard references that influenced Islamic legal and intellectual thought across the Mamluk and Ottoman empires for centuries.
